# Introduction

This file is used to conduct basic correlation analysis on recreational fishers in the 2025 SELTMP data. Pearson's and Spearman's correlations are calculated as matrices between the items in Questions 14, 19, 21, 23, 35, 29, 17, 15 and 24.

The output is organised in three levels:

1.  Question-level overview: one summary matrix showing how strongly each question is related to every other question.

2.  Within-question matrices: item-by-item matrices for each question (Pearson on the left, Spearman on the right).

3.  Between-question matrices: item-by-item matrices for every pair of questions, saved as images, plus a table of the strongest correlations.

All matrices are also exported to one Excel file.

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, include=FALSE}
# R Setup & housekeeping
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
	echo = TRUE,
	include = TRUE,
	message = FALSE,
	warning = FALSE)

rm(list=ls())
objects()
```

```{r}
# Packages
library(tidyverse)
library(readxl)
library(here)
# Hmisc (rcorr) and writexl are called with :: so they don't mask tidyverse functions
```

```{r}
# Settings
adjust_method     <- "BH"   # multiple-testing adjustment: "BH" (false discovery rate)
show_cross_plots  <- TRUE  # TRUE prints all 36 between-question matrices in the document
out_dir           <- here::here("Output")
dir.create(file.path(out_dir, "heatmaps"), recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
```

# 1. Prepare data

```{r}
# Import Raw Data sheet and the variable dictionary
data_file <- here::here("Data/SELTMP-2025-GBR-surveydataset_v1-0_RecFishingCLUSTERS_RyanW-Oct-26-2026.xlsx")

raw_data <- read_excel(data_file, sheet = "Raw_Data")
var_info <- read_excel(data_file, sheet = "Variable Information")

#glimpse(raw_data)
```

```{r}
# Filter Data for only Rec Fishers
# (the previous is.na(inter_zoning) filter is removed: correlations below use pairwise
#  deletion, so each pair keeps every respondent who answered both items)
fisher_data <- raw_data |>
  filter(Are_you_a_Rec_Fisher == 1)

nrow(fisher_data)
```

# Select variables and set all as numeric

```{r}
# Find the variables belonging to each question using the "Variable Information" sheet
questions <- c(14, 19, 21, 23, 35, 29, 17, 15, 24)

q_vars <- map(questions, \(q) {
  var_info |>
    filter(str_detect(Variable, paste0("^q", q, "_"))) |>
    mutate(num = as.integer(str_extract(Variable, "\\d+$"))) |>
    arrange(num) |>
    pull(`Variable short name`) |>
    intersect(names(raw_data))        # drops items that are not in Raw_Data (e.g. q15_19)
}) |>
  set_names(paste0("Q", questions))

# Lookup table: variable -> question -> question text
var_key <- tibble(variable = unlist(q_vars, use.names = FALSE),
                  question = rep(names(q_vars), lengths(q_vars))) |>
  left_join(var_info |> select(variable = `Variable short name`, label = Label),
            by = "variable")

lengths(q_vars)   # number of items per question
```

```{r}
# Numeric data frame used for all correlations
fisher_num <- fisher_data |>
  select(all_of(unlist(q_vars, use.names = FALSE))) |>
  mutate(across(everything(), \(x) as.numeric(as.character(x))))

# Respondents available per item (correlations use pairwise deletion)
summary(colSums(!is.na(fisher_num)))
```

# 2. Calculate correlation matrices

```{r}
# Pearson / Spearman matrices: r, p, n, plus multiple-testing adjusted p-values
run_cor <- function(data, method) {
  res <- Hmisc::rcorr(as.matrix(data), type = method)   # pairwise deletion
  up  <- upper.tri(res$r)
  p_adj <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow(res$r), ncol(res$r), dimnames = dimnames(res$r))
  p_adj[up] <- p.adjust(res$P[up], method = adjust_method)   # adjust across all unique pairs
  p_adj[lower.tri(p_adj)] <- t(p_adj)[lower.tri(p_adj)]      # mirror to lower triangle
  res$p_adj <- p_adj
  res
}

# Convert the matrices to one long table (one row per pair of variables)
make_long <- function(res, method) {
  mat_long <- function(m, nm) as.data.frame(as.table(m), responseName = nm, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  mat_long(res$r, "r") |>
    left_join(mat_long(res$P, "p"),         by = c("Var1", "Var2")) |>
    left_join(mat_long(res$p_adj, "p_adj"), by = c("Var1", "Var2")) |>
    left_join(mat_long(res$n, "n"),         by = c("Var1", "Var2")) |>
    rename(var1 = Var1, var2 = Var2) |>
    mutate(method = method)
}

results <- list(Pearson  = run_cor(fisher_num, "pearson"),
                Spearman = run_cor(fisher_num, "spearman"))

vars <- unlist(q_vars, use.names = FALSE)

cor_all <- bind_rows(imap(results, make_long)) |>
  mutate(unique_pair = match(var1, vars) < match(var2, vars)) |>    # TRUE for one copy of each pair
  left_join(var_key |> select(var1 = variable, q1 = question), by = "var1") |>
  left_join(var_key |> select(var2 = variable, q2 = question), by = "var2")
```

```{r}
# Heatmap function: Pearson (left) and Spearman (right) for any set of rows / columns
plot_cor <- function(rows, cols = rows, title = NULL, labels = TRUE) {
  d <- cor_all |>
    filter(var1 %in% rows, var2 %in% cols) |>
    mutate(label = if_else(var1 == var2, "",
                           paste0(sprintf("%.2f", r),
                                  if_else(!is.na(p_adj) & p_adj < 0.05, "*", ""))),
           r     = if_else(var1 == var2, NA_real_, r),
           var1   = factor(var1, levels = rev(rows)),
           var2   = factor(var2, levels = cols),
           method = factor(method, levels = c("Pearson", "Spearman")))

  p <- ggplot(d, aes(var2, var1, fill = r)) +
    geom_tile(colour = "white") +
    scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#B2182B", mid = "white", high = "#2166AC",
                         midpoint = 0, limits = c(-1, 1), na.value = "grey90", name = "r") +
    facet_wrap(~ method) +
    coord_fixed() +
    labs(title = title, x = NULL, y = NULL,
         caption = paste0("* = significant after ", adjust_method, " adjustment (adjusted p < 0.05)")) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
          panel.grid = element_blank())

  if (labels) p <- p + geom_text(aes(label = label), size = 2.3)
  p
}
```

# 3. Question-level overview

Average absolute correlation between all items of one question and all items of another (the diagonal is the average within a question). Darker = stronger overall relationship.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 6

q_summary <- cor_all |>
  filter(var1 != var2) |>
  group_by(method, q1, q2) |>
  summarise(mean_abs_r = mean(abs(r), na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(q1 = factor(q1, levels = rev(names(q_vars))),
         q2 = factor(q2, levels = names(q_vars)),
         method = factor(method, levels = c("Pearson", "Spearman")))

ggplot(q_summary, aes(q2, q1, fill = mean_abs_r)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", mean_abs_r)), size = 3) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "white", high = "#2166AC", limits = c(0, NA), name = "mean |r|") +
  facet_wrap(~ method) +
  coord_fixed() +
  labs(title = "Average absolute correlation between questions", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank())
```

# 4. Within-question matrices

```{r}
#| fig-width: 13
#| fig-height: 7

for (q in names(q_vars)) {
  p <- plot_cor(q_vars[[q]], title = paste(q, "- correlations between items"))
  ggsave(file.path(out_dir, "heatmaps", paste0(q, "_within.png")), p,
         width = 4 + 0.8 * length(q_vars[[q]]), height = 2.5 + 0.4 * length(q_vars[[q]]),
         limitsize = FALSE)
  print(p)
}
```

# 5. Between-question matrices

One matrix per pair of questions (items of the first question down the side, items of the second across the top). All plots are saved to `Output/heatmaps/`; set `show_cross_plots <- TRUE` in the settings to print them here as well.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 14
#| fig-height: 8

q_pairs <- combn(names(q_vars), 2, simplify = FALSE)

for (pr in q_pairs) {
  rows <- q_vars[[pr[1]]]
  cols <- q_vars[[pr[2]]]
  p <- plot_cor(rows, cols, title = paste(pr[1], "vs", pr[2]))
  ggsave(file.path(out_dir, "heatmaps", paste0(pr[1], "_vs_", pr[2], ".png")), p,
         width = 3 + 0.8 * length(cols), height = 2.5 + 0.4 * length(rows),
         limitsize = FALSE)
  if (show_cross_plots) print(p)
}
```

## Strongest correlations between questions

Top 25 item pairs from different questions, for each method, among those significant after adjustment.

```{r}
top_pairs <- cor_all |>
  filter(unique_pair, q1 != q2, !is.na(p_adj), p_adj < 0.05) |>
  group_by(method) |>
  slice_max(abs(r), n = 25) |>
  ungroup() |>
  arrange(method, desc(abs(r))) |>
  select(method, var1, q1, var2, q2, r, p_adj, n)

knitr::kable(top_pairs, digits = 3)
```

# 6. Export all matrices to Excel

```{r}
mat_sheet <- function(m) as_tibble(m, rownames = "variable")

writexl::write_xlsx(
  list(Variable_key    = var_key,
       Pearson_r       = mat_sheet(results$Pearson$r),
       Pearson_p_adj   = mat_sheet(results$Pearson$p_adj),
       Pearson_n       = mat_sheet(results$Pearson$n),
       Spearman_r      = mat_sheet(results$Spearman$r),
       Spearman_p_adj  = mat_sheet(results$Spearman$p_adj),
       Spearman_n      = mat_sheet(results$Spearman$n),
       All_pairs       = cor_all |> filter(unique_pair) |>
                           select(method, var1, q1, var2, q2, r, p, p_adj, n)),
  path = file.path(out_dir, "Correlation_matrices.xlsx"))
```

# Notes on interpretation

- Pearson vs Spearman: the items are ordinal rating scales (1-5 or 1-10) with many tied values and ceiling effects, so Spearman is the more defensible measure. Pearson is included for comparison; large differences between the two panels suggest skewed or non-linear relationships.

- Missing data: each pair uses every respondent who answered both items (pairwise deletion), so the sample size varies between pairs. The `n` matrices in the Excel file show this.

- Multiple testing: with roughly 4,000 pairs per method, about 200 would be "significant" at p \< 0.05 by chance alone. Stars and filters use adjusted p-values (`adjust_method`); the raw p-values are in the Excel file.

- Direction of items: some items are negatively worded (e.g. `pers_diff`, `sad`, `reef_fatigue`) and are not reverse-coded, so their correlations point in the opposite direction to what the other items suggest.
